stage.name: California Electrical Entrance Exam Prep Courseware
stage.description: Full English OpenMAIC courseware for electrician apprenticeship entrance preparation, diagnostics, instruction, and practice.

scenes.title: Course Goal: Prepare for the Entrance Exam, Not Field Licensing

elements.content: Course Goal: Prepare for the Entrance Exam, Not Field Licensing

This course targets common electrician apprenticeship entrance skills.

You will train math, reading, mechanical reasoning, spatial reasoning, and evidence-based self-planning.

The course uses original practice items and step-by-step explanations.

Do not depend on leaked test questions. Build transferable speed and accuracy.

scenes.title: Readiness Check: What This Course Is For

questions.question: What is the safest preparation strategy when the exact local exam version is unknown?

options.label: Build core skills, then adjust to the official local notice

questions.analysis: Exam structures vary. Core skills plus official local guidance is the most reliable path.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Baseline: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Diagnostic Baseline: What the Exam Is Testing

The first job is to locate weak skills before choosing practice volume.

Target skill: turning a score into a study plan.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Baseline: Core Method

elements.content: Diagnostic Baseline: Core Method

Separate accuracy problems from speed problems.

Mark each missed question by skill, not by page number.

Look for repeated causes: arithmetic slip, setup error, vocabulary, or visual rotation.

Build the next practice block from the largest repeated gap.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Baseline: Worked Example

elements.content: Diagnostic Baseline: Worked Example

A learner misses 5 of 8 fraction questions and 1 of 8 reading questions.

The plan should start with fraction operations, not general test anxiety.

A second short quiz confirms whether the gap is setup, calculation, or both.

Only then should the learner move to mixed timed practice.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Baseline: Common Traps

elements.content: Diagnostic Baseline: Common Traps

Do not call every miss a careless mistake.

Do not study only the topic that feels familiar.

Do not use a full-length test when a ten-question diagnostic is enough.

Do not add speed before the method is correct.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Baseline: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Diagnostic Baseline: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: baseline classification.

Recommended drill: 10 mixed questions, each labeled by skill and error cause.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Diagnostic Baseline

questions.question: A learner misses mostly ratio questions but finishes on time. What should the next plan emphasize?
questions.analysis: The dominant gap is ratio setup, not speed.

questions.question: Which review note is most useful after a missed question?
questions.analysis: A precise error label can drive the next practice block.

scenes.title: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: What the Exam Is Testing

Entrance exams often test whether you can keep operations in the correct order.

Target skill: accurate arithmetic with multi-step expressions.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Core Method

elements.content: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Core Method

Handle parentheses first.

Then multiply and divide from left to right.

Then add and subtract from left to right.

Write one line per operation when the expression is dense.

scenes.title: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Worked Example

elements.content: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Worked Example

Compute 18 + 6 x 3 - 4.

Multiply first: 6 x 3 = 18.

Then 18 + 18 - 4 = 32.

The answer is 32, not 68.

scenes.title: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Common Traps

elements.content: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Common Traps

Do not add before multiplying just because addition appears first.

Do not skip a line when negative signs are present.

Do not use mental math for every step under time pressure.

Check whether the question asks for a value, a difference, or a total.

scenes.title: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: operation order.

Recommended drill: 15 expressions with one written intermediate line each.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Whole Numbers and Order of Operations

questions.question: What is 7 + 5 x 4?
questions.analysis: Multiply first: 5 x 4 = 20; 7 + 20 = 27.

questions.question: What should be done first in 3 x (8 - 2)?
questions.analysis: Parentheses come first.

scenes.title: Fractions: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Fractions: What the Exam Is Testing

Fractions appear directly and inside measurement, ratio, and algebra problems.

Target skill: adding, subtracting, multiplying, and simplifying fractions.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Fractions: Core Method

elements.content: Fractions: Core Method

For addition or subtraction, find a common denominator.

For multiplication, multiply numerators and denominators.

For division, multiply by the reciprocal.

Simplify only after the operation is clear.

scenes.title: Fractions: Worked Example

elements.content: Fractions: Worked Example

Compute 1/2 + 1/4.

Use denominator 4: 1/2 = 2/4.

Then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.

The answer is 3/4.

scenes.title: Fractions: Common Traps

elements.content: Fractions: Common Traps

Do not add denominators when adding fractions.

Do not invert the wrong fraction in division.

Do not convert to decimals if the fraction form is easier.

Watch mixed numbers; convert them before multiplying.

scenes.title: Fractions: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Fractions: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: fraction operation selection.

Recommended drill: four sets: add, subtract, multiply, divide, then one mixed set.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Fractions

questions.question: What is 2/3 + 1/6?
What is 3/4 x 8?

scenes.title: Decimals and Percent: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Decimals and Percent: What the Exam Is Testing

Percent and decimal fluency supports measurement, pay, score, and material questions.

Target skill: converting and using percent change.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Decimals and Percent: Core Method

elements.content: Decimals and Percent: Core Method

Percent means out of 100.

Move from percent to decimal by dividing by 100.

Percent change equals change divided by original value.

Always identify the original value before calculating.

scenes.title: Decimals and Percent: Worked Example

elements.content: Decimals and Percent: Worked Example

A score rises from 40 to 50.

The change is 10.

10 divided by the original 40 equals 0.25.

The increase is 25 percent.

scenes.title: Decimals and Percent: Common Traps

elements.content: Decimals and Percent: Common Traps

Do not divide by the new value unless the question asks for that comparison.

Do not confuse percentage points with percent change.

Do not forget to convert 0.25 into 25 percent.

Read whether the problem asks for increase, decrease, or final value.

scenes.title: Decimals and Percent: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Decimals and Percent: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: percent base identification.

Recommended drill: 10 percent increase/decrease items with the original value circled.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Decimals and Percent

questions.question: A practice score increases from 24 to 30. What is the percent increase?
questions.analysis: The change is 6, and 6/24 = 25%.

questions.question: What decimal equals 12 percent?
questions.analysis: 12 percent means 12/100 = 0.12.

scenes.title: Ratios and Proportions: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Ratios and Proportions: What the Exam Is Testing

Ratio problems test whether you can translate wording into matched quantities.

Target skill: setting up equivalent relationships.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Ratios and Proportions: Core Method

elements.content: Ratios and Proportions: Core Method

Label the two quantities before writing a proportion.

Keep units aligned across the numerator and denominator.

Cross-multiply only after the setup is correct.

Estimate the answer to catch impossible results.

scenes.title: Ratios and Proportions: Worked Example

elements.content: Ratios and Proportions: Worked Example

If 3 boxes hold 48 connectors, how many connectors are in 5 boxes?

48 divided by 3 equals 16 connectors per box.

5 boxes hold 5 x 16 = 80 connectors.

The answer is 80.

scenes.title: Ratios and Proportions: Common Traps

elements.content: Ratios and Proportions: Common Traps

Do not swap the order of quantities halfway through.

Do not cross-multiply a setup you have not labeled.

Do not ignore per-unit language.

Check whether the relationship is direct or inverse.

scenes.title: Ratios and Proportions: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Ratios and Proportions: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: proportion setup.

Recommended drill: 12 direct proportion items with unit labels on every line.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Ratios and Proportions

questions.question: If 4 identical boxes hold 60 parts, how many parts are in 6 boxes?
In a 3:2 ratio with 30 total bundles, how many are in the second group?
questions.analysis: There are 5 total parts; each part is 6; the second group has 2 parts = 12.

scenes.title: Measurement Conversion: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Measurement Conversion: What the Exam Is Testing

Electrical preparation often uses feet, inches, fractions, and simple unit changes.

Target skill: converting units without losing scale.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Measurement Conversion: Core Method

elements.content: Measurement Conversion: Core Method

Write the starting unit and target unit.

Use a conversion factor that cancels the old unit.

Keep fraction inches exact when possible.

Check whether the answer should be larger or smaller.

scenes.title: Measurement Conversion: Worked Example

elements.content: Measurement Conversion: Worked Example

Convert 6 feet to inches.

1 foot equals 12 inches.

6 x 12 = 72 inches.

The answer is 72 inches.

scenes.title: Measurement Conversion: Common Traps

elements.content: Measurement Conversion: Common Traps

Do not multiply when you should divide.

Do not mix feet and inches in the same number without converting.

Do not round too early.

Watch words like radius, diameter, length, and distance.

scenes.title: Measurement Conversion: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Measurement Conversion: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: unit conversion direction.

Recommended drill: inch-foot-yard conversions, then mixed measurement word problems.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Measurement Conversion

questions.question: How many inches are in 5 feet?
questions.analysis: 5 x 12 = 60 inches.

questions.question: Which answer is reasonable for 36 inches converted to feet?

scenes.title: Basic Algebra: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Basic Algebra: What the Exam Is Testing

Algebra checks whether you can isolate an unknown without changing equality.

Target skill: solving one-step and two-step equations.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Basic Algebra: Core Method

elements.content: Basic Algebra: Core Method

Undo addition or subtraction first when isolating the variable.

Then undo multiplication or division.

Do the same operation to both sides.

Substitute the answer back into the original equation.

scenes.title: Basic Algebra: Worked Example

elements.content: Basic Algebra: Worked Example

Solve 3x + 4 = 22.

Subtract 4 from both sides: 3x = 18.

Divide by 3: x = 6.

Check: 3 x 6 + 4 = 22.

scenes.title: Basic Algebra: Common Traps

elements.content: Basic Algebra: Common Traps

Do not move a term without changing its sign.

Do not divide only one side.

Do not forget the final substitution check.

Watch equations with negative numbers.

scenes.title: Basic Algebra: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Basic Algebra: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: equation isolation.

Recommended drill: 20 two-step equations with a substitution check.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Basic Algebra

questions.question: Solve 2x + 5 = 17.
questions.analysis: Subtract 5 to get 2x = 12, then x = 6.

questions.question: What is the best check after solving an equation?
questions.analysis: Substitution confirms the value satisfies the original equation.

scenes.title: Formulas and Substitution: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Formulas and Substitution: What the Exam Is Testing

Technical exams may give a formula and ask you to substitute correctly.

Target skill: using a formula when values are given.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Formulas and Substitution: Core Method

elements.content: Formulas and Substitution: Core Method

Identify the formula exactly as written.

Replace each symbol with the matching value.

Use parentheses around substituted values.

Calculate in operation order.

scenes.title: Formulas and Substitution: Worked Example

elements.content: Formulas and Substitution: Worked Example

Use A = L x W with L = 8 and W = 3.

A = 8 x 3.

A = 24.

The area is 24 square units.

scenes.title: Formulas and Substitution: Common Traps

elements.content: Formulas and Substitution: Common Traps

Do not use a value for the wrong variable.

Do not drop units when the final answer needs them.

Do not change the formula unless solving for another variable is required.

Watch squared units in area problems.

scenes.title: Formulas and Substitution: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Formulas and Substitution: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: formula substitution.

Recommended drill: 10 formula cards: identify variables, substitute, calculate.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Formulas and Substitution

questions.question: If P = 2L + 2W, L = 5, and W = 4, what is P?
Why use parentheses when substituting values?
questions.analysis: Parentheses reduce sign and operation-order mistakes.

scenes.title: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: What the Exam Is Testing

Some entrance items ask you to infer a rule from a table or simple graph.

Target skill: reading change from structured information.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Core Method

elements.content: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Core Method

Read the labels before the numbers.

Find how one quantity changes when the other changes.

Slope is change in output divided by change in input.

Use the pattern to predict the next value.

scenes.title: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Worked Example

elements.content: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Worked Example

A table shows 1 hour = 12 parts and 2 hours = 24 parts.

The output increases by 12 for each hour.

At 5 hours, 5 x 12 = 60 parts.

The rate is 12 parts per hour.

scenes.title: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Common Traps

elements.content: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Common Traps

Do not read a graph without checking the scale.

Do not assume every table is linear.

Do not confuse total amount with rate.

Check whether the question asks for input or output.

scenes.title: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Tables, Graphs, and Slope: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: rate from table.

Recommended drill: table-to-rule problems with one sentence explaining the pattern.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Tables, Graphs, and Slope

questions.question: A machine makes 15 parts per hour. How many in 4 hours?
On a graph, what must you check before reading a point?
questions.analysis: Axis labels and scale tell what the numbers mean.

scenes.title: Reading for Main Idea: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Reading for Main Idea: What the Exam Is Testing

Reading sections test evidence, not personal opinions about trade work.

Target skill: identifying what a passage is mostly about.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Reading for Main Idea: Core Method

elements.content: Reading for Main Idea: Core Method

Read the question first.

Look for repeated nouns and the final sentence.

Choose the answer that covers the whole passage.

Avoid answers that mention only one detail.

scenes.title: Reading for Main Idea: Worked Example

elements.content: Reading for Main Idea: Worked Example

A passage describes cleaning tools, inspecting them, and reporting damage.

The main idea is safe tool return procedure.

A single detail, such as wiping a handle, is too narrow.

A personal opinion about tools is not supported by the passage.

scenes.title: Reading for Main Idea: Common Traps

elements.content: Reading for Main Idea: Common Traps

Do not choose an answer just because it contains a familiar word.

Do not add outside knowledge.

Do not choose an answer that is true but too narrow.

Return to the sentence that controls the answer.

scenes.title: Reading for Main Idea: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Reading for Main Idea: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: main idea evidence.

Recommended drill: short passages with one main idea sentence and one evidence sentence.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Reading for Main Idea

questions.question: What makes a strong main idea answer?
questions.analysis: The main idea must represent the whole passage.

questions.question: Why can a true detail still be a wrong main idea answer?
questions.analysis: A detail can be true but not broad enough.

scenes.title: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: What the Exam Is Testing

Small words often decide the correct answer in workplace-style reading.

Target skill: tracking before, after, unless, except, and required.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Core Method

elements.content: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Core Method

Circle sequence words such as before and after.

Underline condition words such as unless and if.

Treat except and not as direction-changing words.

Answer from the marked phrase, not from memory.

scenes.title: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Worked Example

elements.content: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Worked Example

Passage: Before a tool is stored, it must be wiped and inspected.

Question: What happens before storage?

The answer must include wiping and inspection.

Returning the tool without inspection violates the sequence.

scenes.title: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Common Traps

elements.content: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Common Traps

Do not ignore capitalized EXCEPT.

Do not reverse before and after.

Do not treat unless as optional.

Do not answer from what seems practical if the passage says otherwise.

scenes.title: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Reading for Sequence and Conditions: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: condition and sequence words.

Recommended drill: 20 sentence-level items focused on before, after, unless, except, and not.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Reading for Sequence and Conditions

questions.question: In 'Report damage instead of returning the tool,' which action is replaced?
questions.analysis: The phrase after instead of is the action being replaced.

questions.question: What should you do first when a question contains EXCEPT?

options.label: Circle it and look for the exception

questions.analysis: EXCEPT reverses the usual task.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: What the Exam Is Testing

Mechanical items test simple physical reasoning, often without advanced formulas.

Target skill: using force, distance, and pivot location.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Core Method

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Core Method

Find the pivot or fulcrum.

Identify the force and the distance from the pivot.

Longer distance from the pivot usually creates greater turning effect.

Compare both sides before choosing an answer.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Worked Example

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Worked Example

Two equal weights are placed on a lever.

The weight farther from the pivot creates more turning effect.

To balance it, the other side needs more weight or more distance.

Distance matters as much as weight.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Common Traps

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Common Traps

Do not compare weight alone.

Do not miss the pivot location.

Do not assume the longer side always rises.

Draw an arrow for turning direction.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: lever moment reasoning.

Recommended drill: lever sketches with pivot, force, and distance marked.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Mechanical Reasoning: Levers

questions.question: With equal weights on a lever, which side has more turning effect?
questions.analysis: Greater distance from the pivot creates greater turning effect.

questions.question: What should you identify first in a lever problem?
questions.analysis: The pivot controls distances and turning direction.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: What the Exam Is Testing

Pulley questions check whether you can reason about force and distance tradeoffs.

Target skill: distinguishing direction change from mechanical advantage.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Core Method

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Core Method

A fixed pulley mainly changes pull direction.

A movable pulley can reduce required force.

More supporting rope segments usually mean less force per segment.

The tradeoff is pulling more rope distance.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Worked Example

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Worked Example

A single fixed pulley lets a worker pull down to lift a load up.

The direction changes.

The load does not become weightless.

A movable pulley system may reduce effort but requires more rope movement.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Common Traps

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Common Traps

Do not assume every pulley reduces force.

Do not forget the distance tradeoff.

Do not count the free end as a supporting segment unless appropriate.

Answer whether the question asks force, direction, or distance.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: pulley force-direction distinction.

Recommended drill: fixed vs movable pulley diagrams with support segments counted.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Mechanical Reasoning: Pulleys

questions.question: What is the most typical role of a fixed pulley?
questions.analysis: A fixed pulley mainly changes direction.

questions.question: What tradeoff often comes with mechanical advantage in a pulley?
questions.analysis: Less force often requires pulling more rope.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: What the Exam Is Testing

Gear problems test careful visual tracing from one gear to the next.

Target skill: tracking rotation direction and speed relationships.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Core Method

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Core Method

Adjacent meshed gears rotate in opposite directions.

Insert an idler gear to flip direction again.

Smaller gears usually rotate more times than larger gears.

Trace one contact point at a time.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Worked Example

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Worked Example

Gear A turns clockwise and touches Gear B.

Gear B turns counterclockwise.

If Gear B touches Gear C, Gear C turns clockwise.

The direction flips at each mesh.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Common Traps

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Common Traps

Do not skip the middle gear.

Do not assume all gears turn the same way.

Do not confuse belt systems with meshed gears.

Mark each gear with an arrow before answering.

scenes.title: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: gear-chain tracing.

Recommended drill: three-gear and four-gear chains with arrows drawn on each gear.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Mechanical Reasoning: Gears

questions.question: If two gears mesh and the left gear turns clockwise, the right gear usually turns:
questions.analysis: Meshed adjacent gears rotate in opposite directions.

questions.question: What happens to direction when a third meshed gear is added?
questions.analysis: Each mesh reverses direction.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: What the Exam Is Testing

Spatial items measure whether you can recognize the same object in a new orientation.

Target skill: mentally turning shapes without changing their structure.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Core Method

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Core Method

Pick one anchor feature and track it.

Rotate the entire shape, not one piece at a time.

Check left-right relationships after the turn.

Eliminate mirror images unless the problem allows flipping.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Worked Example

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Worked Example

A shape has a notch on the upper right.

After a 90-degree clockwise turn, that notch moves to the lower right.

The shape is still the same object.

A mirrored notch on the lower left would be wrong.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Common Traps

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Common Traps

Do not confuse rotation with reflection.

Do not track only the outer outline.

Do not ignore a small notch or mark.

Use the same anchor feature for every option.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: rotation versus reflection.

Recommended drill: shape cards rotated 90, 180, and 270 degrees with one anchor mark.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Spatial Reasoning: Rotation

questions.question: What is the key difference between rotation and reflection?
questions.analysis: Rotation turns the object; reflection creates a mirror image.

questions.question: What should you track first in a rotation item?
questions.analysis: An anchor feature prevents losing orientation.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: What the Exam Is Testing

Folding questions test careful adjacency and opposite-side reasoning.

Target skill: predicting where faces and marks meet after folding.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Core Method

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Core Method

Identify the center face first.

Mark which faces touch the center.

Opposite faces cannot share an edge after folding.

Trace symbols through one fold at a time.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Worked Example

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Worked Example

A cube net has a center square with four neighbors.

Those four neighbors fold up around the center.

A square two steps away may become opposite the center.

Use adjacency, not guesswork.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Common Traps

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Common Traps

Do not place opposite faces next to each other.

Do not flip a symbol unless the fold causes it.

Do not judge only by color.

Redraw the net if the answer choices are crowded.

scenes.title: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: folding adjacency.

Recommended drill: cube nets with center, adjacent, and opposite faces labeled.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Spatial Reasoning: Folding and Nets

questions.question: In a cube net, can opposite faces share an edge after folding?
questions.analysis: Opposite faces do not share an edge on the folded cube.

questions.analysis: The center face anchors adjacency.

scenes.title: Word Problems: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Word Problems: What the Exam Is Testing

Word problems combine reading accuracy with arithmetic choice.

Target skill: translating practical wording into math operations.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Word Problems: Core Method

elements.content: Word Problems: Core Method

Underline the requested quantity.

Circle the given numbers and units.

Choose the operation before calculating.

Write a final sentence with the unit.

scenes.title: Word Problems: Worked Example

elements.content: Word Problems: Worked Example

A worker needs 3 lengths of conduit, each 8 feet long.

The requested quantity is total length.

3 x 8 = 24.

The worker needs 24 feet.

scenes.title: Word Problems: Common Traps

elements.content: Word Problems: Common Traps

Do not calculate before identifying the question.

Do not mix units.

Do not answer an intermediate value.

Check if the question asks each, total, remaining, or difference.

scenes.title: Word Problems: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Word Problems: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: word-problem translation.

Recommended drill: 10 word problems with requested quantity, operation, and unit written.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Word Problems

questions.question: A job uses 4 boxes with 25 parts each. What is the total?
Which phrase usually points to subtraction?
questions.analysis: Remaining often asks for what is left after subtracting.

scenes.title: Personal Experience Evidence: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Personal Experience Evidence: What the Exam Is Testing

Some programs ask about work habits, training, attendance, or related experience.

Target skill: turning experience into clear, verifiable statements.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Personal Experience Evidence: Core Method

elements.content: Personal Experience Evidence: Core Method

Use concrete actions, not vague traits.

Name the setting, task, tool, and result when appropriate.

Keep claims honest and verifiable.

Connect the example to reliability, safety, teamwork, or learning speed.

scenes.title: Personal Experience Evidence: Worked Example

elements.content: Personal Experience Evidence: Worked Example

Weak answer: I am hardworking.

Stronger answer: I completed a six-week evening math course while working part time.

The stronger answer gives evidence, duration, and effort.

Evidence is easier to trust than adjectives.

scenes.title: Personal Experience Evidence: Common Traps

elements.content: Personal Experience Evidence: Common Traps

Do not invent experience.

Do not list every job if only one strong example is needed.

Do not use unsafe work as a positive example.

Do not confuse confidence with proof.

scenes.title: Personal Experience Evidence: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Personal Experience Evidence: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: evidence-based application response.

Recommended drill: write three STAR-style examples: situation, task, action, result.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Personal Experience Evidence

questions.question: Which statement is strongest?

options.label: I finished a 10-week evening class with perfect attendance

questions.analysis: It gives specific, verifiable evidence.

questions.question: What should you avoid in an experience response?
questions.analysis: Invented claims create trust and safety problems.

scenes.title: Timed Test Strategy: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Timed Test Strategy: What the Exam Is Testing

A good plan protects easy points and prevents one hard item from taking the whole section.

Target skill: balancing accuracy, pacing, and review.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Timed Test Strategy: Core Method

elements.content: Timed Test Strategy: Core Method

Make a first pass through questions you can solve cleanly.

Mark hard items and return after collecting easier points.

Use estimates to catch answer choices that are impossible.

Reserve final minutes for skipped items and answer transfer checks.

scenes.title: Timed Test Strategy: Worked Example

elements.content: Timed Test Strategy: Worked Example

A 30-minute section has 30 questions.

The rough pace is one minute per question.

If a problem takes three minutes with no progress, mark it and move.

Return after the first pass.

scenes.title: Timed Test Strategy: Common Traps

elements.content: Timed Test Strategy: Common Traps

Do not spend five minutes protecting one point early.

Do not rush so much that you miss simple wording.

Do not leave answer bubbles misaligned.

Do not change answers without a reason from the work.

scenes.title: Timed Test Strategy: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Timed Test Strategy: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: pacing and recovery.

Recommended drill: three 10-question timed sets with skipped-item review.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Timed Test Strategy

questions.question: If one question blocks you early in a timed section, what is usually best?
questions.analysis: Protecting the whole section matters more than one early item.

questions.question: Why estimate before choosing?
questions.analysis: Estimation helps detect scale errors.

scenes.title: Seven-Day Review Plan: What the Exam Is Testing

elements.content: Seven-Day Review Plan: What the Exam Is Testing

The final week should sharpen weak areas while preserving confidence on strengths.

Target skill: turning course results into final-week practice.

Work slowly first. Add time pressure only after the method is stable.

During review, write the exact step where the error happened.

scenes.title: Seven-Day Review Plan: Core Method

elements.content: Seven-Day Review Plan: Core Method

Day 1: diagnostic review and error labels.

Days 2-4: focused drills on the top two weak skills.

Day 5: mixed timed set and explanation review.

Days 6-7: light review, sleep, logistics, and confidence checks.

scenes.title: Seven-Day Review Plan: Worked Example

elements.content: Seven-Day Review Plan: Worked Example

If fraction errors and sequence-word errors dominate, split practice blocks.

Do 20 fraction items, then 10 reading condition items.

Review every miss with a one-line cause.

The next day starts with the same two causes.

scenes.title: Seven-Day Review Plan: Common Traps

elements.content: Seven-Day Review Plan: Common Traps

Do not cram every topic equally.

Do not take a full test every day if review quality drops.

Do not ignore sleep and test-day logistics.

Do not measure progress only by time spent.

scenes.title: Seven-Day Review Plan: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

elements.content: Seven-Day Review Plan: Tutor Diagnosis and Planning

If errors cluster here, tag the gap as: final-week planning.

Recommended drill: make a seven-day calendar from the top two error labels.

Mastery target: 80 percent accuracy before adding speed.

Planning rule: one concept drill, one mixed drill, and one timed mini-set.

scenes.title: Practice Check: Seven-Day Review Plan

questions.question: What should drive the final-week plan?
questions.analysis: The plan should respond to diagnosed gaps.

questions.question: What is a good final-day priority?
questions.analysis: The final day should protect readiness and reduce avoidable mistakes.
